column1: Why is prefill compute-bound and decode memory-bound?
column2: Prefill processes N tokens in parallel (high FLOPs per weight byte). Decode generates one token at a time — arithmetic intensity ~2 FLOPs/byte, far below the H100 ridge point.

column1: What are the three core components of llm-d?
column2: Prefill pods (compute-optimized), decode pods (bandwidth-optimized), and a KV-cache-aware gateway router.

How does KV-cache-aware routing differ from round-robin routing?
column2: It routes requests to decode pods that already hold the request's prefix KV states, enabling cache reuse and eliminating redundant KV transfer.

column1: Why does llm-d handle MoE expert parallelism differently for prefill vs decode?
column2: Prefill activates experts evenly across many tokens; decode at batch size 1 activates experts unevenly. Per-phase EP configuration allows load balancing that monolithic serving cannot provide.

column1: What infrastructure model does llm-d use for deployment?
column2: Kubernetes-native — a Kubernetes operator that manages prefill and decode pod counts, autoscales each independently, and handles KV transfer via pod sidecars.

column1: For a 30:1 prefill/decode token ratio, roughly how many decode pods can one prefill pod feed?
column2: 5–10 decode pods, depending on response length and KV transfer speed.

column1: What is the KV transfer mechanism between prefill and decode pods in llm-d?
column2: A sidecar network buffer manages KV state transfer via NVLink (within node) or RoCE/InfiniBand (cross-node).

column1: What scaling metric triggers prefill pod autoscaling vs decode pod autoscaling in llm-d?
column2: Prefill scales on queue depth (CPU-measured prefill backlog). Decode scales on time-in-decode (long session duration indicates decode pod saturation).
